title: Efficient Autoregressive Inference for Transformer Probabilistic Models
one_liner: Produce coherent joint predictions without re-encoding the whole context at every step by caching the fixed context once and growing a small causal buffer for the targets.
lead: Many set-based probabilistic models are good at answering one target at a time, but many applications need a full joint data pattern over several targets so that the predictions agree with each other. The usual way to get that agreement is costly because the model must repeatedly re-encode the conditioning set after each newly generated target. This paper keeps the context encoding fixed and adds a causal target buffer, which lets the model generate target values one by one while still respecting earlier target choices.

problem.h2: Joint prediction is expensive when the model keeps rereading the same context
paras: Suppose you observe some context points from an unknown function and want predictions at several new inputs. A marginal predictor can answer each new input separately. But a joint predictor must also preserve the dependencies among those answers, because the values at nearby inputs should move together rather than independently.

Set-based models handle context well because they can condition on an unordered set. The cost appears when you generate targets one at a time. After choosing the first target value, the standard method adds that target back into the conditioning set and re-encodes the whole set before choosing the second target. Doing this at every step repeats almost the same work many times.

callout.html: Joint generation is slow because each new target usually forces a full re-encoding of the context set even though the original context has not changed.

panels.title: 1. Fixed context, many targets
panels.caption: The context is stable, but the target list grows one step at a time.

panels.title: 2. Standard method rereads all context
panels.caption: The same context processing is repeated after every new target value.

panels.title: 3. Cache the context once
panels.caption: The stable part is stored and reused because it does not change.

panels.title: 4. Grow a target buffer
panels.caption: Only the growing target side is updated from step to step.

panels.title: 5. Joint samples arrive faster
panels.caption: The model keeps target dependence while avoiding repeated context work.

steps.b: Step 1: Encode the context set once.
steps.text: Read the observed context inputs and outputs into a cached state that stays fixed for the entire target-generation run.

steps.b: Step 2: Create an empty target buffer.
steps.text: Start a causal buffer, which means a left-to-right memory where each target can read only earlier targets.

steps.b: Step 3: Generate the next target value.
steps.text: Each target position reads the cached context and the earlier target states stored in the buffer.

steps.b: Step 4: Append that target to the buffer.
steps.text: Store the new target state so later targets can depend on it without forcing the model to rebuild the context state.

steps.b: Step 5: Repeat until all target values are produced.
steps.text: The context cache is reused each time, so cost grows mainly with the new target work rather than with repeated context passes.

paras: The paper changes where step-by-step prediction state lives. Instead of treating the full conditioning set as something that must be rebuilt after every target value, it keeps the old context fixed and lets only the target side grow.
object.object: the state updated during joint generation

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: repeated context work
hidden.name: context re-encoding count
paras: The main hidden cost is how many times the model rereads the same context points during one joint sample. That number can be large even when the context itself never changes.

The causal buffer lowers that count to one context encoding per run. Later steps still depend on earlier targets, but they get that dependence from the buffer rather than from a full rebuild of the whole conditioning set.

heat.caption: Darker cells show the repeated context passes that the buffer removes.

reads.html: The hidden waste is rereading the same context over and over. The paper removes that waste by caching the context once and updating only the target-side memory.
The causal step-by-step prediction buffer decouples context encoding from target-set growth, so target dependence is modeled without repeated full context recomputation.

mechanism.h2: Why the buffer keeps coherence without repeated full passes
paras: Joint prediction needs two information sources: the fixed context and the already generated targets. The context does not change, so caching it is safe. The targets do change, so they need an updating memory.

The causal buffer provides that updating memory. Each new target reads the cached context for global conditioning and the earlier buffer entries for target-to-target dependence. This works because the model separates what is fixed from what is growing. The fixed part is reused, and the changing part is updated in a small structure whose size tracks only the targets.

stages.s: encode context once and cache it
read cache plus earlier target states
append new target to causal buffer

math.h2: The equation: one context cache plus growing target buffer
math.words: Joint target probability is factorized into a product of one-step probabilities, where each step conditions on the fixed context cache and the earlier generated targets.
math.equation: joint_probability = product over t of p(target_t | cached_context, earlier_targets)
symbols: the target value generated at step t
the one-time encoded state of the observed context set
all target values generated before step t and stored in the causal buffer
the probability assigned to the full target set

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose there are 3 targets to generate.
Step 1 uses the cached context and predicts target 1 with probability 0.8.
Step 2 uses the same cached context plus target 1 and predicts target 2 with probability 0.7.
Step 3 uses the same cached context plus targets 1 and 2 and predicts target 3 with probability 0.9.
Joint probability is 0.8 times 0.7 times 0.9, which is 0.504.
The context was encoded once, but target dependence was still preserved at each step.

math.note: The factorization is standard step-by-step prediction modeling; the paper's contribution is to make the conditioning structure efficient for set-based probabilistic models.

charts.title: Re-encode context each step
charts.note: This baseline preserves dependence but spends most of its time on repeated context work.

charts.title: Cached context plus causal buffer
charts.note: The buffer keeps target dependence while the context cache removes repeated full passes.

items.b: Context that should not be treated as fixed.
items.html: If later targets truly change what the context representation should be, a frozen cache can miss those feedback effects.
If the target list is very long, the buffer itself can become expensive because each new target must still read many earlier targets.
Step-by-step generation depends on order. A bad target order can make early uncertain choices harm many later ones.
Use the cache when the context is truly fixed and choose a target order that matches the dependence structure of the task.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Train a set-conditioned predictor on a toy function-regression task. Then compare two joint-generation modes on the same target sets: one that re-encodes the entire context after each generated target, and one that caches the context once and uses a causal buffer for the targets.
Measure both wall-clock time and joint log-likelihood, because the paper claims the new method saves time without giving up coherent joint prediction.
demo.metric_eq: speedup = time for full re-encoding baseline / time for cached-context buffer method
demo.closing: A convincing demo shows that speedup rises while joint log-likelihood stays close, because the method removes repeated context computation rather than removing target dependence.
